title: Charles Dickens' early life in London

paragraphs.text: In July 1822, when Charles Dickens was ten years old, he moved to London with his family from the county of Kent in the south-east of England. In Kent, Dickens had only recently begun to attend school, and as the summer ended he could not understand why he was not sent to school in London, but kept at home with nothing to do but run boring errands, clean his father’s boots before he set off for work each morning, and look after the younger children. He believed that his parents could have found the money to send him to school if only they had organised their spending better. 'Something might have been spared ... to place me at any common school,' he later wrote. A cousin tried to cheer him up by making him a toy theatre, which Charles loved playing with. His other occupation was writing descriptions of people he observed. He was proud of his writing, but was given no encouragement to write more. His parents were preoccupied with their many young children and with money troubles.

In the spring of 1823, Charles’ sister Fanny was awarded a place at the newly established Royal Academy of Music, and she was to be one of the first boarders. She was 12, and she would be studying the piano with Ignaz Moscheles, a pupil of the well-known composer Beethoven, as well as harmony and singing. The fees were nearly £40 a year, and although Charles claimed that he never felt any jealousy of what was done for Fanny, he could not help but be aware of the contrast between his position and hers, and of their parents’ readiness to pay a considerable sum in fees for her education, and nothing for his. For the next six months, he continued without formal education of any kind, but instead was free to wander around London, learning the layout and character of districts and streets, and observing the contrast between the elegance of Regent Street and the narrow lanes not far from it, where second-hand clothes for sale were hung outside the shops. He was inspired to imagine the life stories of those who had lost worn them, and been reduced to selling them.

The shortage of money in his family led his mother to think how she could put her talents to use, now that her husband’s salary was not growing fast enough to keep pace with the needs of the children. After consulting with friends, she decided on a bold plan: she would run a school. In the autumn of 1823, she took a lease on a large house in Gower Street, and fixed a sign to the wall announcing: 'Mrs Dickens’ Establishment'. The family home was abandoned, along with a pile of unpaid bills, and they moved into the much more spacious house. Charles was sent out with leaflets informing people about the school, and began to hope it might lead to his being sent to school himself. His hopes did not last long. No pupils arrived, and no enquiries were made. All that happened was that John Dickens, Charles’ father, was pursued by creditors with increasing ferocity. Their furious knockings and shoutings at the front door drove John Dickens to hide upstairs, much to his son's shame. Finally his father could hide no more, and he was arrested for debt in February 1824.

John Dickens was taken first to a preliminary place for holding debtors, known as a sponging house. When Charles was sent there by his mother, he was given the role of messenger by his father, to carry his various apologies and requests for help to family and friends. No help came and Charles became frightened. He loved his father, and now saw him about to be taken to a prison for debtors across the river in Southwark. Before he was escorted away, he made a dramatic statement to his son to the effect that the sun was setting on him for ever. Whatever he meant to convey, the child was reduced to despair.

Yet when his mother sent him to visit his father the next day, Charles found his father had cheered up. John Dickens offered Charles the sound advice later credited to a character in one of Dickens’ novels, Mr Micawber: that if you earn £20 a year, an expenditure of slightly less means happiness, but an expenditure of slightly more means unhappiness. Then John Dickens sent his young son to borrow a knife and fork from Captain Porter in the room above, and prepared to settle in comfortably, since he would continue to receive his salary and no longer be pestered by his creditors. There was, he decided, something after all to be said for prison, even though the buildings were old and shabby and there was only a small fire in the room.

In Gower Street things got worse from day to day. Charles, as the man of the family, just 12 years old, was sent out to a pawnbroker*. At first he was sent with the books he loved then with items of furniture, until after a few weeks the house was almost empty and the family was camping out in two bare rooms in the cold weather. All these experiences – debt, fear, angry creditors, pawnbrokers, prison, living in freezing empty rooms and managing on what can be borrowed or begged – were impressed on his mind, and used again and again in his stories and novels, sometimes grimly, sometimes with humour.
